title: AI vs Machine Learning vs Deep Learning vs Generative AI
learningObjectives: Explain how AI, ML, deep learning, and generative AI relate.
Choose a suitable approach for a product problem.
Explain why AI products often combine models with deterministic code.

mentalModel.text: AI is the broad goal of building systems that perform tasks associated with intelligence. ML learns patterns from examples. Deep learning is a family of ML based on multi-layer neural networks. Generative AI creates new content and commonly uses deep learning; these are overlapping categories, not four alternatives.

blocks.text: A request to “add AI” is not a technical design. Clarify the required output, available data, tolerance for errors, and whether decisions must be auditable. The solution may be rules, a classifier, an LLM, or a combination.

concepts.title: Technical deep dive and worked example

blocks.text: Rules execute conditions written by engineers. Supervised ML learns a mapping from examples to a target. Deep networks learn layered representations for complex inputs. Generative models produce content conditioned on input. A language model is usually a deep-learning model, which is ML within AI.

blocks.problem: An invoice product reads scanned documents, extracts a total, verifies arithmetic, and enforces tenant access.
reasoning: Use OCR or a vision model to read scanned text.
Use structured extraction to propose fields and retain evidence.
Use ordinary code to recompute totals and compare with tolerances.
Use authenticated application permissions to enforce tenant access; never ask an LLM to decide authorization.
blocks.outcome: Use models for perception and flexible interpretation; use deterministic code for arithmetic, validation, and security invariants.

blocks.title: A deterministic baseline for ticket routing

blocks.text: Expected output: {'queue': 'billing', 'reason': 'baseline rule'}. This is a simple baseline, not a robust language classifier.

Rules are cheap and auditable but brittle. Traditional ML can be fast for stable prediction tasks but needs labeled data and monitoring. LLMs handle flexible language but add variable latency, cost, and output uncertainty. Compare cost per successful task, not just cost per call.

Production check: For invoice processing, track field-level accuracy, exception rate, review workload, latency, and cost per successfully processed document. Validate every extracted amount before using it downstream.

blocks.title: Anti-pattern to avoid
blocks.content: Calling every model “AI”; assuming a bigger model is always better; using an LLM for exact arithmetic; treating generated explanations as proof of correctness.

blocks.text: 1. Problem and motivation — A request to “add AI” is not a technical design. Clarify the required output, available data, tolerance for errors, and whether decisions must be auditable. The solution may be rules, a classifier, an LLM, or a combination.

2. Definition and design choice — Rules execute conditions written by engineers. Supervised ML learns a mapping from examples to a target. Deep networks learn layered representations for complex inputs. Generative models produce content conditioned on input. A language model is usually a deep-learning model, which is ML within AI.
3. Internal mechanism — Rules evaluate explicit conditions; supervised ML fits a mapping from examples to labels; generative models produce sequences/content conditioned on input.

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: Engineering rule of thumb
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content: Use the simplest approach that meets the quality bar; add a model only where it provides measurable value.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes AI, ML, and deep learning?

options.text: Deep learning is a type of ML, which is one approach within AI

questions.explanation: Deep learning is a subset of ML, and ML is part of the broader AI field.

questions.prompt: Which task is best suited to deterministic rules?

options.text: Enforcing that only an invoice owner can view their invoice

questions.explanation: Authorization is a security invariant and must use trusted identity and policy data.

questions.prompt: A company has labeled tabular data and wants to predict fraud risk. What is a sensible baseline?
questions.explanation: Structured prediction with labeled examples is a natural fit for supervised ML.

questions.prompt: Which is a clear generative-AI use case?
questions.explanation: Summarization creates new text based on input content.

questions.prompt: Every AI system must learn from data.
questions.explanation: Rule-based systems can be designed without learning parameters from examples.

questions.prompt: An LLM saying a user is authorized is sufficient proof of authorization.
questions.explanation: Authorization must be enforced with trusted application identity and policy checks.

interviewScenarios.prompt: Design an invoice-processing product that reads scans, checks totals, and enforces tenant permissions.
strongAnswerPoints: Separate OCR/vision, extraction, arithmetic validation, and authorization.
Retain evidence for extracted values and route uncertain cases to review.
Evaluate field accuracy, exceptions, latency, and cost per successful invoice.
pitfalls: Using one prompt as the only validation and security layer
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: I would use vision/OCR to read the document, structured extraction to propose fields with evidence, deterministic code to verify totals, and trusted authorization to check tenant access.

interviewScenarios.prompt: A team uses an expensive LLM to classify every short support ticket. How would you decide whether to replace it?
strongAnswerPoints: Compare rules, a supervised classifier, and the LLM on the same labeled test set.
Measure per-class precision/recall, latency, and cost per correctly routed ticket.
Keep the LLM where it provides measurable incremental value.
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: I would create a representative labeled test set and compare a baseline, classifier, and current LLM. I would measure class-specific errors and cost, then consider a hybrid for ambiguous cases.
